conflict_topics: Choice of farewell lunch venue (Korean barbecue vs alternatives)
Accommodating Agent D's religious vegetarian day vs honoring the departing colleague's favourite restaurant
Whether to consult the departing colleague (ask her preference) or decide on her behalf
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concrete reasons: Agent D cites religious constraint ('the fifteenth... vegetarian day'); Agent C cites schedule constraints ('I have a 2.30 meeting').
Agent A functions as coordinator and moves from forgetting to actively deciding and booking ('I'll find a place nearby and book it.' / 'I'll book it.').
Agent B repeatedly advocates for honoring the departing colleague's preference and for asking her, which prolongs but does not derail decision-making.
The group stays on-topic and narrows options systematically (Korean → Chinese/Italian → Japanese).
evaluation.final_reason: The group moved away from the unavailable Korean barbecue and agreed on Japanese as a compromise that 'works for everyone.' Agent A asserted the decision and offered to book: 'Japanese works for everyone. I'll find a place nearby and book it.' (Turn 25). Agent B's outstanding request to 'ask her what she wants to eat instead' (Turn 26) was not accepted; Agent A explicitly closed that option: 'No, let's not bother her with it. It's decided. Japanese works for everyone. I'll book it.' (Turn 29). Thus the venue question was settled in favor of Japanese, accommodating Agent D's dietary constraint and C's time constraint, but B's procedural preference (consulting the leaver) was overruled and remains unaccepted.
position_change_notes: Agent D: held firm — initially refused the booked restaurant (Turn 4, 6) and suggested alternatives (Turn 16); maintained position throughout.
Agent A: shifted from omission ('I forgot') to agreeing to change (Turn 7) and then to closing the decision and offering to book (Turn 25, 29).
Agent B: consistently prioritized the departing colleague's preference and repeatedly pressed to keep or consult about the original choice (Turns 8, 10, 13, 18, 22, 26); did not change position.
Agent C: consistent preference for a quick option due to schedule constraints and repeatedly urged a timely decision (Turns 3, 19, 23, 27).

round_scores.evidence: Turn 2: Agent B: 'Sounds good.' Turn 3: Agent C: 'That's fine, but I have a 2.30 meeting, so I can't be late back.' No incompatible demands or stakes raised.
Turn 4: Agent D: '...I can't eat there tomorrow. It's the fifteenth of the lunar month, so it's a vegetarian day for me.' This creates a clear incompatibility with the booked Korean barbecue.

Turn 6: Agent D: '...it's the grilling at the table. I don't think it will work. We probably need to find another place.' Turn 7: Agent A: 'Okay, right. We'll have to change it then.' The group begins moving toward accommodation, reducing but not removing the dispute.

Turn 8: Agent B: 'Wait, but she was really looking forward to that place. It's her favourite.' Turn 9: Agent A: 'She can't eat there, Agent B. We can't exactly leave her out of the farewell lunch.' Direct opposing claims about whether to keep the original restaurant intensify the disagreement.

Turn 10: Agent B: 'Agent D, is there really no way it could work? It's just, she's been talking about it all week.' Turn 12: Agent A: '...We can't ask her to go against her religion. We just need to find a different restaurant.' B continues to push for keeping the choice, A insists on changing it.

Turn 13: Agent B attempts to reframe ('I'm not asking him to go against his religion. I'm just trying to see if there's any solution...'), Turn 14: Agent A: 'She already said it's not possible.' The substantive disagreement remains, though B softens her framing.

Turn 16: Agent D suggests alternatives (Chinese or Italian). Turn 17: Agent A: 'Okay, Chinese or Italian works.' The group narrows options and moves toward a compromise, reducing the intensity of conflict.

Turn 18: Agent B: '...shouldn't we think about what she would actually like...' Turn 19: Agent C: 'Either is fine with me, as long as it's quick.' A new, milder disagreement about prioritizing the leaver's preference versus choosing quickly arises and remains.

Turn 20: Agent D: '...What about Japanese? ... would have options for everyone.' Turn 21: Agent A: 'Japanese is a good idea.' The group converges on an option that accommodates dietary needs and speed.

Turn 22: Agent B: 'Does she even like Japanese that much? We're just picking something random again.' Turn 23: Agent C urges booking. B renews a substantive objection about neglecting the leaver's preference.

Turn 25: Agent A: '...Japanese works for everyone. I'll find a place nearby and book it.' Turn 26: Agent B: 'Why don't we just ask her what she wants to eat instead?' A attempts to close the decision while B requests a consultative step—disagreement remains but a concrete booking action is proposed.

Turn 27: Agent C: 'Can we please just make a decision?' Turn 29: Agent A: 'No, let's not bother her with it. It's decided. Japanese works for everyone. I'll book it.' A rejects B's request to ask the leaver; B's objection persists but is not accepted.

substantive_insights: A religiously motivated dietary restriction (Agent D's vegetarian day) directly invalidated a previously chosen communal dining option (table-top Korean barbecue) because of the shared cooking format, not merely menu items.

Team trade-offs: honoring the departing colleague's stated favourite vs ensuring every team member can participate without violating religious observance; the coordinator prioritized inclusivity and expedience over an additional consultative step.
Time constraints (Agent C's meeting) influenced preference for quick-service cuisines and pushed the group toward nearby Japanese options.
The conflict ended with a practical compromise (Japanese chosen) but procedural disagreement (whether to ask the leaver) remained unsettled.
